claims.text: Participation can remain tokenistic despite an invitation: participants in the empirical framework reported that their input was ignored and management merely claimed it had involved disabled people. NPC recommends active input throughout the process and freedom to disagree with facilitators. (high confidence)

Do not generalize one disabled participant’s input to everyone. W3C warns that experience varies even within one disability; user involvement must be combined with accessibility standards and conformance evaluation because participants cannot cover all disabilities and assistive-technology configurations. (low confidence)

Agree the aims, limits of influence and decision process with participants at the outset. Document collaboration terms in a written agreement, rather than inviting people only after options are polished. (high confidence)

Include people with lived experience early and throughout the process, and consider roles on the project team or as workshop co-facilitators rather than restricting them to late feedback. (medium confidence)

Remote co-design can remove travel demands while introducing inaccessible collaboration tools and connectivity barriers. Select the format around participants’ access needs rather than assuming that moving online makes a workshop accessible. (medium confidence)

Johansson and colleagues explicitly frame their participation framework around impact rather than control, and argue that the quality of participation can be assessed by measures other than power. This scopes stronger claims that co-design always requires maximal participant control. (low confidence)

Plan accessibility across activities, materials and communication, rather than treating venue access as sufficient. The empirical framework describes reading text aloud, sign-language interpreting and slowing discussion; Alfred Health also budgets accessible information, interpreters and spaces meeting physical and sensory needs. (high confidence)

Co-design gives participants influence over problems, ideas and decisions. Asking for feedback while others retain decisions is consultation; research participation alone does not establish co-design. (high confidence)

Budget for participants’ time and the costs of participation. Choose payment arrangements that work for participants, and include access support, suitable venues and accessible materials in the budget. (medium confidence)

Adapt workshop conditions and materials to participants, and revise them from feedback. Reported failures include rooms without microphones or loudspeakers, inaccessible materials and presentations that move too quickly; the practitioner guide recommends describing visual aids and providing different ways to contribute. (medium confidence)

Make decisions traceable through written collaboration terms, shared workshop summaries, and explicit communication of design limitations and trade-offs. This is an operational synthesis of the sources’ transparency guidance, not a prescribed decision-log format. (medium confidence)

Attendance alone is insufficient evidence of meaningful influence. In the empirical study, participants described being invited without having their input taken into account; the accessible co-design guide recommends being honest about what can change and the barriers to change. (medium confidence)

Do not promise that co-design is always the best or cheapest approach: MIT D-Lab says it can cost more than alternatives and is not a silver bullet; Mural identifies time, resource, decision-making and equitable-participation challenges. (medium confidence)

Choose meaningful participatory roles: Alfred Health recommends people with lived experience on the project team and as workshop co-leaders or co-facilitators, with support and training; NPC also proposes participants helping decide what and how to evaluate. (high confidence)

Budget appropriate compensation for participants’ time and expertise. Alfred Health recommends flexible payment arrangements that work for each person; participants in the empirical framework study described reimbursement as recognition of equal partnership. (high confidence)

For online co-design workshops, Alfred Health recommends accessible agendas and joining instructions in advance, sufficient time for activities and questions, description of visual aids, and multiple ways to contribute, including speaking, chat and visual cards. These are facilitation recommendations, not proof that any particular platform is accessible to everyone. (low confidence)

Keep a traceable feedback loop: NPC recommends explaining what the team heard and changed in response to participants. The empirical framework additionally recommends communicating design trade-offs and limitations to the whole team. (high confidence)
